query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high-temperature, self-healing tribo‐ceramic coating—such as a doped TiO2-based layer—on the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy surface will enable it to maintain low friction and wear rates from room temperature through 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Bare CoCrFeNi alloy that performs adequately at room temperature but degrades at higher temperatures due to oxidation and microstructural softening, leading to increased friction and accelerated wear.
generation.intervention: Depositing a doped TiO2-based self-healing tribo-ceramic coating on the CoCrFeNi substrate.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted under controlled normal loads in ambient air, with temperature varied from approximately 25 °C (room temperature) to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The coating facilitates the formation of a continuous, dense glaze-like oxide layer that self-heals during sliding, thereby protecting the underlying substrate from oxidation and abrasive wear.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures the coating provides a low-shear, engineered surface that minimizes friction. As temperature increases, the dopant promotes self-healing oxidation, leading to the formation of a stable, protective tribo-ceramic glaze that reduces adhesive and oxidative wear, thus maintaining low friction and wear across the temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the uncoated CoCrFeNi alloy, the coated material is expected to show a significantly lower and more stable friction coefficient and reduced wear rate consistently from room temperature to 800 °C, with marked improvement at high temperatures where the bare alloy typically degrades.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi HEA without any surface modification, which shows increased friction and wear due to oxidation and softening at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Temperature: 25 °C to 800 °C; Load: typical sliding wear test loads; Environment: ambient air.
generation.uncertainty: The precise formulation and adhesion of the coating may require optimization. In addition, long-term thermal cycling could challenge the integrity of the self-healing glaze, and the quantitative improvement margins (e.g., percent reduction in friction) are not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of bare CoCrFeNi HEA specimens and a second set coated with the doped TiO2-based self-healing tribo-ceramic layer. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests at incremental temperatures from room temperature (≈25 °C) to 800 °C under a fixed normal load in ambient air. Monitor real-time friction behavior and post-test wear through microscopy.
measurements: Friction coefficient as a function of temperature
Wear volume or wear rate post-testing
Surface characterization (e.g., SEM, XPS) to confirm formation and stability of the glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate at high temperatures (e.g., above 600 °C) relative to the uncoated specimens, or if the self-healing, dense glaze layer is not observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

frame.system: CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix used for sliding contact applications
frame.goal: To achieve a consistently low coefficient of friction and low wear rate over the full temperature range (room temperature up to 800 °C)
frame.limitation: The baseline CoCrFeNi alloy experiences performance degradation, with increased friction and wear due to temperature‐induced changes (such as oxidation or microstructural softening) that make it difficult to maintain uniform tribological performance across a wide temperature range.
root_cause_cues: difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate
constraints: a single intervention must be applied
operation and testing conditions include sliding contact from room temperature to 800 °C
the intervention must perform under specified load and environmental (likely ambient air) conditions without requiring additional external controls
frame.regime: Sliding wear tests performed under controlled loads in an ambient environment, spanning temperatures from approximately 25 °C (room temperature) to 800 °C
prior_attempts: Baseline assessments of the CoCrFeNi matrix showed that while it performs adequately at lower temperatures, its tribological properties degrades at high temperature due to oxidation and microstructural changes
Previous strategies may have targeted either room‐temperature or high‐temperature performance individually, but not both simultaneously

families.principle: Modifying the surface—by applying coatings or creating engineered tribo-films—can provide a protective barrier against oxidation and wear while directly contributing to low friction, independent of the substrate's bulk properties.
cues_for: difficulty maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate during sliding
the full temperature range implies that any beneficial surface film must operate from room temperature to 800 °C
prior attempts that focused on the CoCrFeNi matrix alone encountered performance degradation, suggesting the surface could be the key intervention point
cues_against: Although coatings can be vulnerable to wear, proper design (e.g., self-healing or graded coatings) may adequately address the challenges posed by sliding and high temperatures.
families.best_lever: Develop and apply a high-temperature, self-healing tribo-ceramic coating (for example, a doped TiO2 or similar material) that maintains low friction and wear performance across the entire temperature range.

families.principle: Optimizing the processing conditions (such as rapid solidification or additive manufacturing parameters) can refine the microstructure, leading to grain size reduction and improved phase homogeneity, which may enhance tribological performance.

families.best_lever: Adopt rapid solidification techniques to produce a finer, more homogeneous microstructure which could mitigate microstructural softening at elevated temperatures.

families.principle: Designing a favorable microstructural architecture (such as dual-phase structures or embedded hard second phases) can improve load distribution and resistance to wear.

families.best_lever: Engineer a dual-phase microstructure with in-situ formed hard reinforcements to strengthen the matrix and reduce wear.
